rounds.text: Modison Ltd is drastically under-appreciated by the market, trading at a modest P/E of 11x [E1] while delivering extraordinary fundamental performance, including a trailing twelve-month profit growth of 209% [E21] and a 3-year compounded profit growth of 83% [E20]. This exceptional profitability is supported by elite capital efficiency, boasting a phenomenal ROCE of 28.61% [E10] and an ROE of 29.57% [E9], both of which vastly outperform their respective sector benchmarks of 11.86% and 9.61% [E9, E10]. Valuation metrics further emphasize this disconnect, with the company's EV/EBITDA sitting at a negligible 4.75x compared to a towering sector benchmark of 329.57x [E11]. A discounted cash flow model suggests massive intrinsic mispricing, leaving a staggering margin of safety of 70.8% [E46], whereas a reverse DCF reveals that the current share price only requires a paltry 1.0% earnings growth to be justified [E47]. Operational tailwinds are firmly intact as well, demonstrated by operating margins expanding to 25% in Mar 2026—a 13 percentage point increase over the year-ago quarter [E31]—and a rules-based quantitative engine scoring the stock a near-perfect 99 out of 100 with a high-confidence BUY rating [E63]. Conceded: operating cash flow for Mar 2026 is negative at Rs -64 Cr [E35], resulting in a weak cash conversion ratio of -0.88x against reported profit [E34].

Despite reported profit growth, Modison Ltd suffers from severe cash flow erosion, with operating cash flow plunging to negative Rs 64 Cr and free cash flow dropping to negative Rs 79 Cr in March 2026 [E35, E36]. This disconnect results in a dismal cash conversion ratio of -0.88x against reported profit, with operating cash flow representing a negative 36% of operating profit [E34, E37]. Compounding these liquidity concerns, borrowings have more than doubled to Rs 174 Cr in March 2026 up from Rs 73 Cr the previous year, elevating debt to equity to a moderate 0.64x [E38, E39]. Furthermore, official warnings note that the company might be capitalizing interest costs, casting doubt on the true quality of its earnings [E62]. Quarterly operating margins are also flagged as inconsistent over the last two quarters [E33], while the stock itself carries a high annualised volatility of 57.5% alongside a historical peak-to-trough drawdown of -48.8% [E53, E54]. Conceded: the company displays strong trailing profit growth and an attractive P/E ratio [E1, E21].

Conceded: operating cash flow was negative Rs 64 Cr and free cash flow dropped to negative Rs 79 Cr in March 2026 [E35, E36]. However, this cash friction sits alongside exceptional fundamental profitability, with a trailing twelve-month profit growth of 209% and a 5-year profit CAGR of 26% [E19, E21]. The heavy investment phase reflects aggressive scaling, evidenced by compounding sales growth accelerating to 45% over the trailing twelve months and 29% over three years [E16, E17]. Furthermore, institutional money flow remains positive with foreign holdings increasing, and a rules-based screen awards the stock a high-confidence 99 out of 100 score [E42, E44, E63]. While borrowings rose to Rs 174 Cr, the debt-to-equity ratio remains at a manageable 0.64x, backed by elite returns on capital employed reaching up to 31% [E12, E38, E39]. Finally, the market drastically underappreciates these operational dynamics, as the current price implies a mere 1.0% future earnings growth against an 18.0% base-case assumption [E47].

Conceded: trailing twelve-month profit growth reached 209% and the 5-year profit CAGR is 26% [E19, E21]. However, citing this profit surge ignores the severe warning that operating cash flow collapsed to negative Rs 64 Cr and free cash flow dropped to negative Rs 79 Cr in March 2026, producing a cash conversion ratio of -0.88x [E34, E35, E36]. While the bull points to aggressive scaling and accelerating sales [E16, E17], this top-line expansion coincides with a stark negative cash flow representing -36% of operating profit [E37]. Furthermore, the bull downplays the financial risk of rising borrowings, which jumped from Rs 73 Cr to Rs 174 Cr in a single year [E39], accompanied by a specific flag that the company might be capitalizing its interest costs [E62]. Although foreign institutional holdings and rules-based screens are highlighted [E42, E44, E63], they do not neutralize the concrete accounting reality of negative cash generation, a moderately leveraged debt-to-equity ratio of 0.64x [E38], and high annualised volatility of 57.5% [E54]. Finally, the implied earnings growth derived from reverse DCF models [E47] cannot override the immediate fundamental danger of a business consuming massive cash [E35, E36] while aggressively ramping up debt [E39].
